title: Micro-offload tiering and probabilistic early termination for OOM resilience
creator: Marcus Li
description:
Problem: High-tail request patterns and very long-prefix chat sessions intermittently push GPU memory beyond available limits. Existing strategies (hard eviction, model fallback, and coarse-grained KV trimming) either cause large quality regressions or produce noisy retry storms. We need a low-latency, low-quality-regression approach that reduces OOM frequency and provides controlled recovery when OOMs happen.

Proposal summary: Implement a two-pronged approach: 1) micro-offload tiering — aggressively slice cold KV and ephemeral tensors to host memory in small, prioritized slabs; 2) probabilistic early termination — a token-level, model-aware signal that gracefully truncates or summarizes low-utility tail tokens under memory pressure and then retries on a lighter path. The system will be complemented by fast checkpoint/restore of KV shards and deterministic fallback to a quantized, smaller replica model for the remaining generation when necessary.

Key components and behaviors: 
- Micro-offload tiering: maintain per-request KV residency score and split into hot slab (GPU), warm slab (pinned host memory), and cold slab (page-backed or compressed storage). Sliced residency is at ~64–512KB slabs to avoid giant DMA ops. Offload happens proactively when model lifetime or batch admission predicts memory contention.
- Probabilistic early termination (PET): during generation, compute a low-cost utility score per token (combines logprob delta, repetition heuristic, and user-configured len_penalty). Under memory pressure, PET applies a probabilistic function (seeded to be reproducible per request) that decides per-token to: (a) end generation early with a concise summary; (b) request a model-side continuation on a smaller model; or (c) emit a flagged partial response and schedule a background retry on a cheaper path.
- Fast KV shard checkpointing & restore: before slab eviction, write minimal KV snapshots (delta-encoded) to a per-GPU NVMe pool (or host memory if NVMe unavailable) and store pointers in request context to allow sub-second restore.
- Lightweight model hedging: if restore or retry latency is likely to violate SLO, route remaining generation to a quantized 1/2-size variant (same tokenizer, distilled head) with a calibrated bias to preserve intent.

Metrics and targets: reduce OOMs by 70% for long-session 95th percentile; keep mean token-latency regression < 10% on affected requests; measured quality drop (ROUGE BLEU/semantic-sim) for truncated responses <= 6 points for experimental prompt set.

Decision trade-offs: 
- Host offload increases latency for cold tokens but avoids catastrophic OOMs; by slicing small slabs we limit tail latency spikes.
- PET trades some output completeness for availability; we make this opt-in per-customer and provide quality hooks for Redwood Optimize to tune thresholds.
- Checkpointing to NVMe is durable but increases I/O tail; prefer host RAM when strict latency SLOs apply.

Operational considerations: 
- New telemetry: per-request slab map, offload/restore latency, PET invocations and outcomes, fallback model usage, and end-to-end retry counts. Expose as per-route rates in Console.
- Rollout: start as a binary feature behind runtime flag; enable for low-SLA hosted routes first, then test on dedicated pools.
- Safety: mark PET responses as partial in API metadata (response.partial=true, reason), include reconstructability pointers.

Implementation plan (high level): 
1) Kernel & runtime: implement slab allocator for KV and ephemeral tensors + host offload DMA path (ENG runtime team).
2) PET service logic: implement token-level utility heuristic and probabilistic decision function in the runtime:lightweight control path.
3) Checkpoint store: extend existing NVMe snapshot API to support delta shards and quick restore.
4) Fallback model infra: small-model packaging, quantization profile validation, bias calibration harness.
5) Instrumentation + Console dashboards + rollout flags.

Acceptance criteria: see acceptance_criteria field.

Known risks: increased complexity in memory accounting and potential for I/O storms; we will rate-limit offloads and add backpressure circuit breaker.

comments: 2026-02-26: Kickoff meeting — aligned on slabs (256KB target) and PET seed determinism. Action: runtime team to prototype slab allocator (Marcus).
2026-03-02: Early prototype demo — host-offload works on synthetic long-prefix workload but adds ~70ms median for cold-slab restores. Noted opportunities: compress slabs before NVMe write (LZ4).
2026-03-05: Design review — PM asks for per-customer opt-out and explicit partial-response flag. Security reviewed offload metadata (no PII checkpointing).
2026-03-08: Engineering update — implemented delta-encoding for KV shards; integration tests added. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4682
2026-03-10: QA run — PET reduced OOMs in experiment by 62% on internal chat dataset; follow-up to tune probabilistic parameters. PR for PET: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4721
Next steps: schedule canary on hosted-low-sla pool, add Console charts for offload rate and PET frequency, and run customer-facing A/B with opt-in flag.
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end canary shows >=70% reduction in GPU OOM events for long-session cohort (95th percentile) compared to baseline
Latency P50 for affected requests increases <10%; P95 tail regressions are capped via backpressure circuit breaker
Partial/PET responses are clearly flagged in API and restore path is documented for customers
Restore/evict cycle succeeds with 99% correctness in operator-run chaos tests
Fallback quantized model produces acceptable semantic fidelity on the Redwood internal prompt set (rating >= 0.85 vs baseline embedding cosine)
